claims.claim: F.broadcast and hint('broadcast') give BroadcastHashJoin; with broadcasting off, SortMergeJoin; autoBroadcastJoinThreshold defaults to 10 MB; AQE is on by default; explain supports mode='formatted' with PushedFilters.
claims.source: Run on PySpark 4.0.4 in this repository.

claims.claim: Databricks recommends liquid clustering over partitioning for UC managed tables; serverless does not support cache APIs.

concept_html:
A join between two large tables needs a shuffle: Spark moves rows across the network so equal keys meet on the same executor, then sorts and merges them. The plan shows this as SortMergeJoin with Exchange steps. Shuffles are the most expensive thing Spark does.

When one side is small, such as a lookup of 200 region codes, Spark can broadcast it: send a full copy to every executor and join locally, with no shuffle of the large side. The plan shows BroadcastHashJoin.

  • Spark broadcasts automatically when it estimates a side is under spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold, 10 MB by default in Spark 4.0.
  • Adaptive query execution (AQE), on by default, can switch a join to broadcast at run time once it sees real sizes.
  • You can force it with F.broadcast(small_df) or small_df.hint("broadcast"). Do this for lookups you know are small. Never broadcast something that grows with your data.

Read the plan before you tune. df.explain() prints the physical plan. df.explain(mode="formatted") adds details per step, including PushedFilters, which confirm that a filter reached the file scan.

Partitions decide parallelism.

  • repartition(n) shuffles to exactly n partitions. coalesce(n) merges partitions without a shuffle, and only reduces the count.
  • repartition(1) or coalesce(1) before a large write puts all the work on one task. Avoid it outside tiny outputs.
  • For table layout on Unity Catalog managed tables, prefer liquid clustering over partitionBy. If you do partition a table, choose a low-cardinality column such as wave_id, never an ID.

Caching: df.cache() helps on classic clusters when several actions reuse a result. Serverless compute does not support it. There, write the intermediate result to a Delta table.

lines: def enrich(fact, regions):
regions_local = regions.collect()
lookup = {r.region_code: r.region for r in regions_local}
label = F.udf(lambda code: lookup.get(code), "string")
out = fact.withColumn("region", label("region_code"))
return out.repartition(1)

solution_lines: from pyspark.sql import DataFrame
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
def enrich_with_regions(fact: DataFrame, regions: DataFrame) -> DataFrame:
"""Left-join fact rows to the small regions lookup, broadcasting the lookup."""
return fact.join(F.broadcast(regions), on="region_code", how="left")
def unmatched_codes(enriched: DataFrame) -> int:
"""Rows whose region_code had no match in the lookup."""
return int(enriched.agg(F.count_if(F.col("region").isNull())).collect()[0][0])

title: Joins, broadcast, partitions and reading the plan
why_html:
A gold job joins 40 million respondent rows to a 200-row region lookup. Auto-broadcast does not kick in, because the lookup is read through a view whose size Spark overestimates. Every run shuffles all 40 million rows across the cluster, and the join takes 22 minutes.

explain() shows SortMergeJoin with two Exchange steps. Wrapping the lookup in F.broadcast() turns it into BroadcastHashJoin, and the join drops to under two minutes. Five minutes reading the plan saved twenty minutes on every run.
